newsitem.title: MALDIVES: S.Asian leaders urge political talks to end mistrust.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian leaders urge political talks to end mistrust.

text.p: Leaders of seven South Asian nations began a summit on Monday with calls for more political dialogue among members to end the mistrust that has restrained economic growth.

"We (should) institute a separate but parallel process of political dialogue for the purpose of further consolidating understanding and harmony among our countries," said Maldivian President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom.
Such talks would make more effective the role of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) as a "confidence building mechanism," he told the opening session of the summit.

SAARC comprises the Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island nations of the Maldives and Sri Lanka, mostly Hindu India and its Moslem majority neighbours, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

The association's charter prohibits the discussion of contentious bilateral issues that could hamper regional co-operation at its official forums but the summits provide for "retreats" that allow informal face-to-face talks among leaders.

Gayoom's call for more political dialogue was echoed by Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga who suggested more frequent, informal and confidential talks among SAARC leaders during their summits.
"Our tangible achievement to date has been relatively insubstantial," she said. "What has held us back was a lack of sufficient political will."
Kumaratunga also urged member states to accept the reality of asymmetry in size and power within SAARC and the pivotal position of the largest member, India.

The opening day of the three-day conference was dominated by a meeting between the prime ministers of the region's two biggest states, India and Pakistan, whose rivalry has frustrated SAARC's efforts to pull the region out of poverty.

"We're deeply conscious of the need to free South Asia of mistrust and hostilities," Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif said. "The dividends of success will be enormous not only for Pakistan and India but also for the entire SAARC region."

Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said the meeting later on Monday with Sharif would help the two nations quickly establish neighbourly relations, and that he was very encouraged by his counterpart's comments.
The ninth summit will focus on ways to speed up growth in member states of the 12-year-old bloc, which represents 1.2 billion people or one fifth of the world's population.
SAARC leaders acknowledged that progress towards economic integration had been slow and agreed to launch a review to revitalise the regional grouping.

They also urged an end to non-tariff barriers that have held back efforts to increase cross-border commerce. Trade among member states stihl accounts for only three percent of their total world trade.
Gujral called for "across the board tariff reductions" to establish free trade in South Asia by the turn of the century.
The region's annual per capita income of $309 is the lowest in the world, and lags behind sub-Saharan Africa's $555, according to the Islamabad-based Human Development Centre.
SAARC leaders also called for measures to enhance the role of women and protect children as well as the environment.
